utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber received this morning another clipping from a newspaper, 19th of March, 1992. It seems that it also is from Politika. It's now -- can't see what page it is, but it has got something to do with the referendum, Cutileiro, from what I understand from the heading of this article, and attached to it is a page we saw before. It has been distributed to the parties, Mr. Krajisnik, so that they can decide whether it assists -- whether it assists them in the course of the examination or otherwise, and then we'll hear from the parties whether they want to tender it. Mr. Krajisnik, I was informed that you'd like to add something to your testimony of yesterday and you could do it in two minutes. Please proceed. But not until after I have reminded you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I only wish to say that I'm concerned by the way I'm being

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: material that I'm seeing for the first time. Let me take for example the club of deputies of the 28th of February. It says explicitly what Jovan Cizmovic was tasked to do, but I didn't know about it. And it is constantly being put to me that his task was the implementation of Variants A and B. And I can give you the number. Second, it makes mention of the document, that study prepared by the economic institute concerning the feasibility of the state of Krajina. Mr. Cizmovic says here that he gave his own report rather than somebody else's to Mr. Karadzic and me. That's all I wanted to say. I don't think this is the proper way to get at the truth. Instead, it only leads to wrong conclusions. I have reviewed this, and I can say that all the conclusions drawn yesterday are completely wrong because I was not familiar with the document, and I can point out to the things that I believe are wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if the way of questioning is improper, I expect your counsel to intervene. Second, if you say I see for the first time the document regarding the club of deputies, you now say, I didn't know about it. I think no question has been put to you as to whether you were present at that meeting. So, therefore, if you were not present, or at least if that's unclear, then it does not come as a surprise that you wouldn't know about it. Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify. I believe that Mr. Krajisnik was saying he was unfamiliar with the club of deputies meeting or that he wasn't present. I think we addressed that before. I think he was talking about the document Mr. Cizmovic was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Then I misunderstood that. But most important, Mr. Krajisnik, Defence counsel will have an opportunity to further question on these matters. Conclusions were not drawn yesterday by this Bench, and that's I think most important. Of course, and that is part of the procedure followed in this Court, that the Prosecution is allowed to put to you documents, to put to you inferences they think these documents would justify to make and then to seek your answers to those matters. This does not allow you to tell us everything you know. Your first -- we expect you first to answer those questions. As I said before, at the very end, you'll have an opportunity to add something. And again, if the questioning is improper, I expect your counsel, who know, of course, the rules, the technical rules of examination of witnesses, that they will object to the way you are examined. But we listen carefully to you, and if it comes to decisions to be taken on whether and to what extent you can expound on the questions put to you by the Prosecution, I'll keep that certainly, and the Chamber will keep that certainly in the back of its mind. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, can we begin by having Mr. Krajisnik presented again with several maps, including D7. The maps depicted in the Politika article, I think is D247. And I'm sorry, my mistake, Your Honour. The Politika article received the number P1194.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, as we discussed yesterday, P1194 depicts three maps which you've described as the proposals of the three parties, and from top to bottom, the Serb, Muslim and Croat maps. D7 contains a map -- or depicts a map that you've described as the Muslim map. And I'd like to look at three areas of both of those maps in somewhat more detail. So if we look at the middle map on P1194, the Muslim proposal. Let's look in particular at three municipalities. And perhaps that can be put on the ELMO so that we can ensure we are all talking about the same municipalities at the same time. If we can first -- if we look at the Muslim map, please? Thank you. That's fine. And Mr. Krajisnik, is there a pointer available to you or a pen that you can use to point out some aspects? Can you point to the Court where Cajnice and Rudo are, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rudo is here, and Cajnice is also here. Here is on the extreme, Rudo and Cajnice should be one of these two. I cannot quite make it out. So Rudo and Cajnice are in this part here.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And as we can see from the legend, those are shaded portions which were part of the areas that fell within the Muslim area, according to this map?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot explain the Muslim map. It was put there as the Muslim map, and it's unclear. You see it says "Muslim map" here. I can only explain the Serb map, and I can explain the Cutileiro map.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to explain beyond it, Mr. Krajisnik. I'm just pointing out these areas, and the Court can determine from the legend itself and from the shading which areas were claimed within -- claimed to be within the boundaries of the particular national group according to that map. And if you could also point out Sekovici to the Court?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sekovici should be -- I really can't make anything out here, but I think Sekovici is somewhere here, right.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Sekovici is there. Sorry, maybe a little further above, here.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: All right. Well, and again, where you pointed, we can see from the shaded portions of the map and the legend that appears on the map that that would be a Muslim area according to this map. Now, if you would turn quickly to D7. Put that on the ELMO as well, sir, or if the usher would. And look again at those same three municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Rudo and Cajnice, the Serb part. This is Sekovici. And the rest, let me see. The rest is mainly the same, but I don't see on this -- Sekovici is not marked as Serb territory on the Muslim map. Rudo and Cajnice is marked as not Muslim, because this entire part here is Muslim, apart from the Croat enclaves.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: That's -- that's correct. And specifically referring to those three municipalities, we can see that they are marked as Serb areas. And in fact, in 1991, according to this the census, those three municipalities were majority Serb?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And, in fact, this entire map reflects the municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina according to the absolute and relative majorities in those municipalities; correct? In so far as you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see exactly whether it's all correct, but I suppose it is, if you took the entire municipalities into account, not individual parts of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Which, of course, is precisely what the statement on principles indicated was annexed to it, that is, a map reflecting the absolute and relative majorities, and as you knew from before, from the very first time this issue came up and the Prosecution presented it, this map was provided to the Prosecution by Mr. Cutileiro.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could have this marked, Your Honour. And it should be distributed as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1195, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this -- needs a number? It's not in evidence yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the statement of principles is in evidence, Your Honour. The annexed map is in evidence. There was representation made in court or -- and a discussion in court about the fact that it had been provided by Mr. Cutileiro and only including the first -- the cover page, for completion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So now we have the combination together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it comes from Mr. Cutileiro, from what I see on the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. And as I mentioned before, that was the subject of discussion between the parties much earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And if we could turn also to tab 84 --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But may I say something with regard to this map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If -- I want to -- us to look at the record from the 16th Session of Republika Srpska where Karadzic says Cutileiro gave us a border on the Una River, and that proves that this is not the Cutileiro map because there is no border on the Una River here. And it's not Cutileiro's map; you have proof of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, let's go through it in all detail. I tend to agree with you that we have to make some distinctions. First of all, what map has been attached to the statement of principles, what happened during further negotiations, and the mere fact, and I'm stressing the mere fact, that Mr. Karadzic says something is not 100 per cent proof of that being correct and something else that contradicts that is not correct. Just to -- not to say that Mr. Karadzic was not telling the truth but just to say that matters are not as simple always as they seem at first sight. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the article at tab 84, from Oslobodjenje on 19 March will need a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1196, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in front of you now is, as indicated, an article from Oslobodjenje of 19 March 1992. The headline says: "Agreed but not signed, three Bosnias." And as you can see, there is a large picture of a map. We have also provided a clearer version of that and a blowup of that as well for ease of reference for the Court and the parties. As you can see from the caption under the map, Mr. Krajisnik, it states: "Map offered as part of the document and is the basis for the work of the group formed with the aim to define the territories of constitutive units." And, again, looking more closely at that map, and you may find it easier to distinguish the shading if you look at the last two pages provided, we can see again that Cajnice, Rudo and Sekovici fall within what is described as Serb territory, consistent with the absolute or relative majority population in those municipalities as in the other municipalities depicted in that map. So this is a contemporaneous reflection of the fact that the map that was annexed to the statement of principles of March 18th, 1992 was a map as stated explicitly in the principles themselves reflecting the absolute and relative majorities of the municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map that we looked at just now was a Muslim map. The Muslim newspaper, Oslobodjenje, depicted it as a map discussed in Lisbon or in Sarajevo, I'm not sure. This is not Cutileiro's map. I claim with absolute certainty that it's not Cutileiro's map.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Because you've claimed with similar absolute certainty that the map that was under discussion or that was attached to the statement of principles was a map that dealt with territorial units smaller than municipalities, such as settlements; indeed, settlements. That's it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that the map that I showed is Cutileiro's map. D7, whatever the number was, not this one that you are showing me now, because I know that. I know that, I saw that map, I participated in that.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Well, clearly the map in the Oslobodjenje article, the map in -- that is D7, are maps reflecting municipality breakdowns, maps that are distinguished by municipalities --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, could Mr. Krajisnik clarify whether he means D7 or D7B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took it that he referred to D7B.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's how I understood his answer. He was uncertain about the number but it is the map --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- saying in Cyrillic "Cutileiro."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that the question was not -- thank you, though, for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: I just want to -- let's try to get that clear. So the map in the Oslobodjenje article, the map that we've looked at this morning, in focusing on Cajnice and Rudo and Sekovici, those are maps of municipalities, right, and the map that you were talking about during the course of your examination-in-chief at length was, as you explained to the Court, a map that was based on territorial units smaller than municipalities, based on settlements?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map that you mentioned first, that's the Muslim map, you're right on that. Muslims opted for a relative or absolute majority, whatever, I don't know what they wanted, and it has to do with municipalities; whereas the Cutileiro map did not rely exclusively on municipalities. That is to say, municipal borders. Because there is the territorial principle, the economic principle, and the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Seems to be some confusion. The first map, Mr. Krajisnik, as you said, was introduced by Mr. Tieger, as far as I understand, as a map just depicting population majority in municipalities, rather than Muslim map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to make the chronology clear, Your Honour, the map we've been -- the map that I presented to Mr. Krajisnik first this morning, along with the maps shown in the Politika article, was labelled D7. That's because it came up during the course of, I think, Mr. Treanor's testimony, if I remember well, and it got a marking by the Defence. But it was during the course of the Prosecution's case, so if there is any confusion about that, I didn't want that to be left unclear. And, yes, that's the map to which I was directing my questions now and asking Mr. Krajisnik whether or not it's a map based on municipalities and that the distinctions between the Serb, Muslim and Croat areas are rendered on the basis of municipalities. So I think we can see that from the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we in one way or the other come to the core of the matter? The core of the matter seems to be that Mr. Krajisnik says the map I pointed at, that's D7B, was the starting point Mr. Cutileiro gave us for further negotiations, whereas you say the only thing Mr. Cutileiro did and that appears from the statement of principles is that he gave a map just depicting in what municipalities which nationality had a majority, yes or no. I mean that seems to be the issue. Mr. Krajisnik insists on D7B to be the map attached to the Cutileiro Plan. You insist to say -- well, in your questioning you very much insist on Mr. Cutileiro presenting the other map as being attached to the statement of principles. I'm very curious to know if Mr. Krajisnik is right, the question what D7B is has been answered. If Mr. Krajisnik is not right, I'd like to know where D7B comes from. Do you -- because you take the position that Mr. Krajisnik is, at least that's the line of your questioning, is not right -- as the map attached to the statement of principles, do you know -- do you have any idea where it comes from and could that -- if so, could that be included in your questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the answer is, Your Honour, I can't enlighten the Court on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we -- there is a difference of view, and we have newspaper articles, we have a card of Mr. Cutileiro, we have the statement of principles which gives some clue. We have a couple of --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I offer one more clue that I was about to ask about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: I had an opportunity, Mr. Krajisnik, to examine the Politika article that you provided. It was about to be translated, as we discussed yesterday, and we did get some of it translated. And at page 1, we see some comments by Dr. Karadzic who says at the bottom of page 1, and Mr. Krajisnik, you will find that quote at the last column to the right in the article, about the third paragraph down, where Dr. Karadzic says: "It is obvious that others have had their own maps, although only the Serbian Democratic Party has been accused of making maps. They have existed for a long time, based on the present municipal borders. It was proposed to set a framework which will contain the undisputed municipalities while the contested places will be determined by a work group that will deal with cartography." So on the 18th of March, the date of the statement of principles, Dr. Karadzic appears to confirm that the map that was to serve as the basis for further discussions, the map that was annexed to the statement of principles, was a municipal map, or a map based on municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I admire you, Mr. Prosecutor. I assure you that the map that I showed you is the Cutileiro map. There are 20 documents where it is recorded. Believe me, there is a brochure, there is papers where it was recorded when no one ever knew of The Hague Tribunal and now, if that is in dispute in this court, that is a big time problem. I assure you that Karadzic was referring to the eastern part because there is no corridor there. I don't know what he meant. But on the map, the Una was the border, on every map. Look this up. That's what Cutileiro did. Look at other agreements too. So, of course, this is not the Cutileiro map, the one that he provided then.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Well, speaking about settlements and areas of land or areas broken down in units smaller than municipalities, you indicated that that was based in part, or reflected very closely, the ownership of land, which was a part of the basis for the claims made by you and the other Bosnian Serb leaders involved in the negotiations. Is that a -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that one of our arguments is the area that was held by the Serbs, 64 per cent or whatever. I don't know whether that's the actual figure but that's the figure that we used. You're right. That's why we got 49 per cent, half of Bosnia. We didn't get 30 per cent, which would be the population ratio, or 35 per cent or 33 or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, it was known, not -- first of all, the Muslims strongly disputed that, and there were even discussions in the Assembly reflecting the fact that the Muslim side strongly disputed that claim by the Serbs and even submitted studies that they felt demonstrated the contrary. So that dispute existed, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall any study. As for the Muslims disputing this, that's true. They always kept saying, how did the Serbs do that math? So you're right on that. But I tell you that the land survey office gave us these figures in this map. I haven't got any studies or -- I don't know of any other thing. I just know what I heard and that is what we used as an argument. But probably a land surveyor or whoever could calculate this.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And there were even Serbs who asserted that that position was incorrect and even ridiculed that position; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember such Serbs. If there are such Serbs, I really wonder at you. I did not observe any Serbs who ridiculed that but possibly, possibly some individual did that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I would like to remind the parties that we are spending an enormous amount of time at this moment on one matter which seems to be in dispute. That is, with what map Mr. Cutileiro sent the parties, the three parties at that time, into further -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting, but if it's of any use to the Court I was moving on. I didn't have another question about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, it's worthwhile to spend one minute on it in order to avoid this to happen again. We spent an enormous amount of time on -- with what map Mr. Cutileiro sent the parties to further negotiate. It's clear that in the answers of Mr. Krajisnik the emphasis was laid on agreement reached on the principles which he considered very important, whereas the fact that further negotiations were needed was very much emphasised in the questioning by the Prosecution. It is also clear that at least we heard quite some evidence that the Muslims withdrew from further negotiations and did not want to start these further negotiations on the basis of the statement of principles. Now, whether the starting point for something that has never really started was more or less favourable and whether you would have a view on that, whether that is of such vital importance for this case that it would justify so much -- such a great amount of time spent on it is a question which I would not answer easily by a yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before my learned friend does that, very, very briefly, I'd like to turn to something Your Honour said really at about the bottom of page 10, top of page 11 of LiveNote today, when Your Honour said, asked in effect what the Prosecution was saying about map D7B. Much of this confusion, in my submission, might be helped if the Prosecution put their case to Mr. Krajisnik, because for my part it's still not clear exactly where this cross-examination was going. If they put the case robustly to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I try to express what I -- I understood the Prosecution's case to be that -- first of all, that Mr. Cutileiro did not give anything else to the parties than a map depicting in what municipalities, what ethnicity or what nationality had a majority, and that any claim that Mr. Cutileiro took already a more favourable position to the Serbs by pointing at map D7B is incorrect. Is that a proper understanding of what your case is, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As stated in my own words, Your Honour, I think what we -- the Prosecution's case was, in -- first of all in response to an enormous amount of time spent on D7B during the course of Mr. Krajisnik's evidence, with linkage to a variety of subsequent events and actions and the assertion during the course of the Defence case that that was the map that was annexed to the statement of principles and therefore an agreement. The Prosecution's case was -- is that the map that was annexed to the statement of principles was precisely what it said in the statement of principles, the map of the absolute and relative majorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and not D7B.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And do the Prosecution have a case as to where D7B has come from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked him already and I didn't receive any positive response to that. But, of course, if it is the position of the Prosecution, right or wrong, that it was another map, then, of course, the Prosecution is not under an obligation to tell us where D7B comes from. If it is -- if they are right. Just as the Defence is not in a position to tell us why it was anything -- D7B.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I accept that entirely. I submit what the Prosecution needs to do is say to Mr. Krajisnik, D7B is a figment of your imagination, or whatever their case is. Put the case robustly. That's what I invite my learned friend to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well -- yes. In another way, it was robust but I leave it to Mr. Tieger whether that's -- I mean, it's clear if D7B was not attached to the statement of principles, then it must come from somewhere else, and until now, although I specifically asked for it, no one could tell me that it came -- the Prosecutor can't tell me that it comes from -- well, that it comes from somewhere else but not from where, and, of course, from Mr. Krajisnik, there is no reason to give any such explanation because he says it comes from the statement of principles. So the mystery is unsolved, and I think in view of the questions -- of the answers given by Mr. Krajisnik, that there is no -- really no need to make it more robust than it is already. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, I'm reluctant to take any more time on this particular issue than has already been consumed. However, I think it needs to be put in context, especially when there is an assertion that the Prosecution is not putting its case to the witness. Of course, the Prosecution case, as the Court knows, during the course of our case in chief was not about the Cutileiro Plan. Instead this issue came to the fore during the course of the Defence case when it suddenly emerged as an explanation for a great deal of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the events, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And so the Prosecution is responding to a few elements of that. And it should not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed and see what your next question is.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to turn from the maps and turn as quickly as we can to the principles. As the Court noted and suggested earlier, the extent to which the Bosnian Serb leadership accepted those principles and the extent to which it -- any of those principles may have been incompatible with Bosnian Serb objectives, and in that connection, if I could turn to tab 81. Which will need a number, Your Honour. It's a tape recording of the 49th Session of the RS Assembly held on 13 February 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1198, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Turning to page 116 of the English, and page 02153828 of the B/C/S version, Mr. Krajisnik, the beginning of the second paragraph of that page. This is Dr. Karadzic speaking saying: "The first position in all Cutileiro's principles, if you remember, was that Bosnia was a state consisting of this and that, but it always said that Bosnia was a state and we never accepted that, and we demanded the maximum that we could accept, Bosnia is a confederation of states, if we have to stay in some kind of a federation, but our minimum is that our state is a state and that it cannot be drowned in anyone else's statehood and sovereignty, except for the statehood and sovereignty of the Republic of Serbia, if we so wish, not even Yugoslavia, because if it's Yugoslavia, then we want to preserve our federal unit, our state as a federative unit of this federation, even though our priority was to become a part of Serbia." Mr. Krajisnik, was Dr. Karadzic correctly stating the Bosnian Serb position, that the statement of principles was, in insisting that Bosnia was a state, was inconsistent with Bosnian Serb objectives to ensure that Republika Srpska was a state and had its own sovereignty?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a difference between a state and a state union. I gave you this morning this document where Cutileiro says there were certain terminological problems that we bypassed deliberately, we circumvented them. We had accepted for Bosnia and Herzegovina to be an internationally recognised entity, a member of the United Nations, but what form it would take was subject to agreement. We wanted a confederation. So it could have only been a Republika Srpska within Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's written here. And the name is on the -- on par with names like Bavaria, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for clarification of the record, at 10.10.48, line -- it's page 26, line 23, where it says "federation," I either misread confederation from the text or it wasn't picked up. But in any event that word should be "confederation." Mr. Krajisnik, was it or was it not the case that irrespective of the steps along the path to that goal, that had to be temporarily that might have to be temporarily accepted, the Bosnian Serbs' objective was to establish a separate state and then unite all Serb states?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not correct. That was rhetoric. I've already said this. We had accepted from the outset to be within Bosnia as a separate entity, and that's the only truth. And whenever there were times of crisis, we used that rhetoric. Otherwise, in all plans, Republika Srpska was to be within Bosnia, and we stated that.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: All right. So the repeated assertions to the effect that I've just stated about the insistence on a Bosnian Serb state and the unification of all Serb states, when they appear in the 11th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly or in any other sessions or public appearances, your assertion is that was mere rhetoric, in order to obtain the objectives of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely. Because one can see in negotiations what it is we were working for, and we had to serve that plan to the deputies.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And what about more privately, in talking to colleagues who were close to you personally and who you had a chance to share your views on the need for or determination to obtain a Bosnian Serb state? Did you -- sorry, did you use political rhetoric with them as well or did you tell them what you thought?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In private conversations, people always voiced their wishes, and it was always the wish of the Serb people not to be separated from the rest of the Serb people. However, the policy we conducted was real politik [phoen] and we always reckoned with Bosnia being an internationally recognised entity, a state, with Republika Srpska in it.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Let me ask you about one telephone conversation not directly involving you but about you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It will be distributed and needs to be marked, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1199, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I missed the number, Mr. Registrar. It doesn't appear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, P1199.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this is a conversation between Zika and Kole, who was we know from previous evidence was Mr. Tintor. And if you'll look at the beginning part of the conversation, we can see Mr. Tintor and Mr. Zika talking about negotiations. And so we can see from the date these were the continuing Cutileiro negotiations that resulted in the statement of principles on March 18th, 1992, a week after this conversation. Mr. Tintor says: They wanted to force them into signing. Had MK not been there, it would have turned into major trouble. Zika: What happened? Tintor: MK saved the day. What did they want to sign, says Zika. Tintor: Well, they persisted ... he says they had seven hours long confrontations, man ... yes ... and Doktor was ill. Zika: Yes. Tintor: And MK said, the lord may strike me down dead, but it can certainly not be sovereign. And then they had a showdown, and they told him he was stubborn and an imbecile ... and they called him names, whatever you can think of. They were all over him, for God's sake, he says he was afraid. And then it goes on to talk about the pressures and difficulties of negotiations. And then if we can turn to page 4 of the English. And, Mr. Krajisnik, I believe that will be on -- at the bottom of page 4 of your version, continuing on to the next page. And in the English it begins about the fourth passage from the top: Tintor: So help me God, you know how much I appreciate my best man MK, he's more than a brother to me. I told him, my man, God forbid that you sign such a thing, or else I'd have killed yourself and the Doktor and NK, and God grant I never saw my children again. That's my opinion, no one has the right to betray the Serbian people. He said: I'd have killed myself, if I had to do that. There is no God up in the sky and no devil beneath the sea that could make me do it, he said. There'd be no need to kill him. He would have killed himself. And then Zika says: They must have offered them marks. And Tintor: Everything, man, the whole world, he said, we can get killed, all of us, what's the matter with you. Zika: Fuck it, man, they are real Serbs then, they are. Tintor: Well, until he's ... until it's -- he alone can negotiate ... nothing more ... no one is to be authorised except him and Doktor. All the rest can go to hell. Hats off to you, Professor NK, and these other ones, all of them are able and let them remain down there where they are, but in negotiations, there is no one but him and Doktor, no one else. Zika: Exactly, exactly. Tintor: There is no third one, and there need not be a third one. Zika: Exactly. Mr. Krajisnik, you recall that conversation with Mr. Tintor that he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean a conversation with me?

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Tintor is referring -- seems to be referring to a conversation with you. Do you recall that conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. It's possible that I had a conversation with him but I don't recall it. But I can say what happened at this session on the 11th of March, at the conference.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Well, I'm not interested at the moment in the details of that session, that particular session in March, but whether or not you in fact told Mr. Tintor that Bosnia and Herzegovina will certainly not be sovereign, and that you'd -- there is no force on earth that could -- or in heaven that could make you sign something that would give Bosnia and Herzegovina sovereignty, if you were expressing your real position or just engaging in political rhetoric?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there was nothing for me to sign. That's a mistake. I don't know how Mr. Tintor interpreted that. I cannot remember the whole conversation with him. I can only remember what happened at the conference. As to that conversation with him, if I had any conversation with him, I cannot remember what it was about. But the references to the conference seem to be correct. Because I'm not the one who signed agreements. There was nothing for me to sign. Karadzic could have signed something or not signed something.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Okay. I asked you a moment ago about Bosnian Serb objectives and whether -- whether or not certain positions taken or accepted during the course of negotiations were simply steps along a path to a longer-term goal. It's the case, isn't it, Mr. Krajisnik, that from rather early in the existence of the SDS, at least from 1991, the Bosnian Serb leadership had a sense of where it was going and steps planned to take along the path toward a Bosnian Serb state?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is complicated. I would have to be more specific. I just cannot understand the point of your question, whether we had anything of our own. Of course, we had our own vision of -- I don't get it. We had certain visions as to what we want, but just tell me more specifically what you're aiming at and then I'll try to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: That's not a problem. You merely have to say that, and if the question lends itself to any problems I'll certainly reframe it. You told us earlier that the actions taken by Bosnian Serbs, such as regionalisation, for example, were reactions only to steps, to actions taken by the other side. And I'm putting to you that in fact the Bosnian Serb leadership had in mind the steps it wanted to take and merely waited for the Muslim side to do certain things in order to put those actions into effect, in order to give either seeming legitimacy to their positions in the eyes of the international community or to use actions taken by the Muslims to inspire the Bosnian Serb people to follow the SDS. They weren't reactions, they were planned out steps.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not. And I would have been happy if you were right, if we were such a smart people as to outsmart the Muslims and foresee their steps.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Well, maybe you'll tell me again this is political rhetoric, but I would ask you to turn next --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I, however, explain that conversation you asked me about, the conference of the 11th of March? You need to understand why I was opposed, as this man seems to convey, the agreement of the 11th of March.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, we are just about to hit a break, I see. Secondly, the answer, as far as I'm concerned, is no. I asked you that question and showed you the intercept because I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the intercept but, of course, in order to better understand. Mr. Krajisnik, if you could do it in approximately one minute, to be as concise as possible, please explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, one minute. We had reached an agreement that we recognise Bosnia and give up on the idea of Yugoslavia. After that, we were served a proposal that did not meet those requirements. It did not give us a constituent unit. And the assembly later rejected that agreement. However, I didn't attend that session because they had attacked me in advance at the conference saying that I would put the assemblymen off accepting that agreement, that I would dissuade them from accepting it. Milanovic was there. Milanovic was chairing the session instead of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to think about it but reserve our position. I may take the same point in relation to P1199 that I did in relation to P1193 yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You mean context and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, not being used as part of the Prosecution case, is the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We've heard already some of the response by the Prosecution. We'll hear from you if the matter comes up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We haven't heard the Prosecution's response. But, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They gave it to us as a glance but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't think they have yet. But I agree, I can discuss that very topic with Mr. Harmon at the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be a good idea. Then before we break, Mr. Krajisnik, you added one element to the discussion of what was the starting point Mr. Cutileiro sent you to further negotiate, and you said Mr. Karadzic said that we got certain territory, I think it was somewhere at the border, and that appears from the 16th Assembly Session, that's the 12th of May session. If you could -- I'm not asking for any further explanation. I'm just asking for you to point exactly what -- where to find in the 16th Session specifically where Mr. Karadzic said that -- perhaps you could find that during the break or think about it and then tell us after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That he said that the Una was the border, that that's what Cutileiro gave us? Just give me the 16th Session and I'll find it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the reason why I raised the issue. Could the B/C/S version of the 16th Assembly Session be provided to Mr. Krajisnik during the break? We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's turn into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I invited you to point at the specific page where I find in the 16th Assembly Session -- so I'm not seeking at this moment any further explanation but, first, to spot exactly where to find Mr. Karadzic's remark.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 00847723 is the page. The fourth strategic objective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a look at it. Thank you very much. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I can just have one moment to look at the English version of that, as long as we are on the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see it's on page 13 of the English. And it literally says -- working maps proposed at the last session, I don't know exactly what had been the last session prior to the 12th of May, but it could have been the 18th of March.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just trying to see what it says at this moment. "The European Community recognised the border on the Una, that is then one of the two rivers mentioned in the fourth strategic goal." This is my observation. "They marked the Una as our wartime border and painted everything east of it blue." Mr. Krajisnik, what was the last session before the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to say something. I want to correct myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to be of assistance. I said that I would be telling the truth here. That is the Cutileiro map, the one that I said. But it seems that there was a session in Lisbon after the 18th of March, so possibly at that session, well, I don't know, but perhaps at that session this map was presented. I don't want to say anything that would be a sin but perhaps there was this other map. Because they say here the last session. As far as I know, it was the 27th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What possibly may have been the case is -- comes easily to speculation. Mr. Krajisnik, you said that we would find in the 16th Assembly Session that Mr. Cutileiro had given -- and I have to reread.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- at least, I mean, it's so easy to verify that. There is nothing on my mind which would think of you trying to deceive us because -- I mean, if ever. I find you intelligent enough not to do it, in such a way, because it could be verified easily, but it does not exactly say here what you said it would say. So therefore, it causes me to ask you also to be very precise in whatever reference you make to documents or other sources. Mr. Tieger, you made proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it says here that the Una is the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it says, as a matter of fact, that "they," and that is the European Community, "marked on working maps proposed at the last session the Una River as our wartime border," which I don't know whether Mr. Cutileiro drafted wartime borders or -- but it needs at least some further thought before we can -- but it's certainly -- you pointed at this source as being of relevance for -- for the whole of that map issue and that's clear to us now. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to have this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, excuse me, it doesn't say "they." It says "the European Community." That's what is written here, "the European Community." At the last session, et cetera. Not "they." "The European Community." I'm sorry, I beg your pardon. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you had earlier said that Mr. Cutileiro did something and I pointed that it was the European Community. Whether that's the same is a matter that we could consider. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, before the break I had asked you about steps taken by the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Serb leadership, and in that connection I would like to turn to a portion of the 38th Session of the RS Assembly held on 17 January 1994. I think that may need to be distributed. Your Honour, this needs a number, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1200, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, and -- sorry. I believe that ours should be P1199. The previous exhibit marked as P1199 had a number that was P762, tab 6, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. So now the extract of the 38th Session would be P1199.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For what it's worth, Your Honour, I had agreed with my learned friend I was going to withdraw my objection to it in any event. That was before I knew that it was part of the Prosecution case, and I think Your Honour will hear later, perhaps from my learned friend Mr. Harmon, about P1193.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if I could direct your attention to the -- basically the third page of the English but the first written page or -- that's in English and also the first page of your version, at the -- toward the bottom, beginning at about seven lines from the bottom on 02152234. And also, Your Honours, beginning in the last four lines of the first page in English, where Dr. Karadzic states: "Let us use Alija's mistake to increase the price of wine. Remember how all the SAOs and all those measures before the war always took place following Alija's mistakes. There were nine to ten actions that we carried out. We brain-stormed them all together. However, we did not pull all nine moves straight away. But we carried them out after Alija made a mistake. It is then that we would make a move. And the Muslims would curse his mother afterwards and not ours. We have to let the Muslims make a mistake so that the world could say, well, what do those Muslims want? They have been offered 33 per cent. Europe requested 30 per cent. We consented to 30 per cent at this Assembly." And then Dr. Karadzic continues discussing the percentages and that the difference in the percentages does not come at Serb expense but at the expense of, in that case, the Croats. As I indicated, before the break, I had asked you a question related to precisely that, whether or not the Bosnian Serb leadership had in mind the steps to be taken and waited for the Muslim side to make certain, as they called it, mistakes, before implementing each of those steps.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I will give you many examples, proving that we did not know where the Muslims would make mistakes, and I'll give you many examples from 1991 up to the end of the war. I can also explain what Karadzic was saying.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Well, first of all, is Dr. Karadzic accurately recalling the anticipated actions, the brain-storming, and the sequential moves made by the Bosnian Serbs, or is this more political rhetoric, according to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're misinterpreting what Karadzic said. He said very nicely, remember how we took moves that were the result of brain-storming, that were well thought out, after every mistake made by the Muslims. Now, that's in the past. And now, what, again we are supposed to wait for the Muslims to make a mistake, if they make a mistake, because they agreed on 33 per cent of the territory and then they gave up on that. All of that is written here. We did not know what the Muslims would do. We could not anticipate that or foresee that in any way.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And that would -- that explanation, Mr. Krajisnik, would appear to ignore Dr. Karadzic's remark that "we did not pull all nine moves straight away but only after Alija made a mistake."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic says, "We made nine moves." That's in the past. But we did not make these moves straight away. As a mistake was made, we would make our move. He did not say, "We thought of nine moves, and then we took these moves when Alija made mistakes." So now he's saying to Vjestica, "Let's not do what you're suggesting but if the Muslims make a mistake, then let's do that." That is the essence of what he's saying. I can say that every time we were surprised and then we would go on thinking and discussing this for a long time after every one of these mistakes that was made.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Let's turn next then to the shorthand notes of a meeting of the Presidency of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia held on 9 December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it needs a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1200, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: First of all, turning to page 2 of the English, and page 04663374 of the B/C/S, Dr. Karadzic begins by saying, "Yes, the constitution is being" -- before I begin that, let me ask you, Mr. Krajisnik, if you were present at this meeting with Dr. Karadzic on the 9th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that I was present. I can't remember but then I probably was present. I thought that I was not there but it says here that I was. That's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic [Realtime transcript read in error "Dragan Kapetina"] says, "Yes, the constitution is being violated and now, therefore, it's accepted because the Krajinas have existed for so long and have become a reality. You can see the behaviour of Europe. When it's suitable, Europe accepts legality. When not, it doesn't accept legality but the factual status. Therefore, we have to be wise enough and prepare both legality and the factual status. We always have to act from the standpoint of legality and of factual status. We have to be that way because that's the way Europe is, inconsistent, that is consistent in following its own interests." And somewhat -- just a little bit farther down, about four lines down, Dr. Karadzic starts -- or speaks about moves. "We have made a list of moves, ten moves in the direction we want, so that there are results. Bosnia remains in Yugoslavia, either as a whole or in our areas, but we won't do anything until Alija messes up. When Alija messes something up, we make move number 5 and then we wait. When Alija messes something else up, we make move number 6. For example, we held the plebiscite now. Had we held it when our hawks suggested, not more than 60 to 70 per cent of Serbs voted but since we waited for Alija and that illegally adopted memorandum and then announced the plebiscite, even people on their death-beds got up to vote, so we must all play the same string." Now you explained Dr. Karadzic's -- I see it, Your Honour, at page 41, line 19, it says Dragan Kapetina, and I'm certain I said Dr. Karadzic and, of course, that's what the transcript of the session reflects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the record now.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you explained Dr. Karadzic's remarks about the nine to ten moves in 1994 as being moves only taken and brain-stormed after the so-called mistakes of Mr. Izetbegovic were made. But we see here in 1991, before all the moves were made, that Dr. Karadzic says we have made a list of the moves. Ten moves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we invite Mr. Krajisnik to answer this question, your first question to Mr. Krajisnik was did you attend this meeting? And then Mr. Krajisnik said, I don't remember, but it states my name. Of course, I looked at the English version. I didn't find anything yet. Then I -- my attention was drawn by the first line which says "part of text untranslated." In the original, it seems that there is a list of those present and the time, I take it, at which the meeting started, quarter past 1.00 in the afternoon. However, Mr. Krajisnik, if you say my name is there, so although I don't remember, I don't see your name. Could you tell us where you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you have no recollection. And, Mr. Tieger, unless I overlooked something the document as such does not, as was more or less accepted by Mr. Krajisnik, the answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I made a mistake. You're right. I see here President of the Assembly, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There were lots of presidents of assemblies but from other -- other bodies. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, when Dr. Karadzic is referring in 1994 to a list of nine to ten moves that had been brain-stormed -- that we had, as he said it, brain-stormed together but did not pull all of them out straight away, that was a list of moves that had been prepared by the time of this meeting on December 9th, 1991, and the Bosnian Serb leadership was waiting for the opportunity to pull those moves out, to implement those moves. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assure you, Mr. Prosecutor, that that is not the case. We had a policy, and then we made our moves after something had been made incumbent upon us to do. Every time they did something, it was a surprise for us. I will explain to you that we could not have foreseen any one of the moves made by them.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: What was the list of moves that Dr. Karadzic was talking about at the beginning of December 1991, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what list this is. I know what we were doing, so maybe it was nine or ten. I can tell you all the things that we did by way of counterproposals to some of their moves. I can explain all of that to you. I think I've already said that but I can repeat it. And also, why we did not know in advance that they would make a particular move.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: I was not suggesting to you, Mr. Krajisnik, that you were in a position to predict the particular moves that Mr. Izetbegovic would make, and I don't read anything in the text that suggests that Dr. Karadzic was saying he was in a position to predict the precise moves they would make. Instead he was saying the Bosnian Serbs had prepared a list of moves and would wait until certain opportunities presented themselves before implementing one after the other. And so I asked you: What was that list?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assure you that there was no such list. There were just some thoughts as to how to deal with certain things and to get out of some situations. As for the proclamation of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I'm going to tell you how that happened and you will see that we did not plan anything in advance. I'll show you that on that one particular example and on any example, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: I don't believe that's necessary, Mr. Krajisnik, particularly after I indicated to you that I wasn't suggesting that you were -- that the list was necessarily dependent upon the particular moves that the Bosnian Muslim leadership took. If the Court wants to hear it, I'm at their disposal of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the Court would like to hear this further explanation, we'll let you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Can we turn next to tab 42, please. I'm sorry, tab 86. My apologies. Sorry, the two tabs were stuck together, so it's tab 87.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Already in evidence, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There is an inversion on the list, Your Honour, so I needed to make sure the Court has the -- is looking at the same document I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 87 is a Serbian television, Colonel S, recording of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then it's tab 86 in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 86 seems to be the -- from what I see, the 42nd, although it's not translated, 42nd Session of the Assembly of the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska, 18th and 19th of July, 1994. Oh, yes, it says minutes and tape recordings. It's a stamp on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct. And if we could -- it does need a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1201.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn first to page 5 of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krajisnik, that would be -- that would correspond to 02152883 of the B/C/S, beginning at the very end of the fifth sentence from the bottom. And, Your Honours, on page 5 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that, yes, that's the same five, four lines from the bottom, 18th of March. Is that where we start?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic speaking saying: "When we won the battle for our republic on 18 March, we won it on 18 March, thanks to Mr. Krajisnik's skills." He continues talking about the length of the talks. Says: "So when the Muslims agree that there would be three Bosnias on ethnic basis, they should call us and then we would agree to it." Then continuing on the next page in English, and the next page on your version, about six lines down from the top of the page, in English, and --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the next one, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: That's right. And about eight lines down, eight or nine lines down for you, Mr. Krajisnik. "That was the first time that Alija" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, sorry, I didn't follow. Can you just tell me which line? Because I've found the passage referring to Cutileiro's map.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Excuse me, you want to be on page 881 --

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: 84, yes, that's right. Ten lines down, beginning in -- you'll see the word "Alija" there in the middle of the sentence. "That was the first time that Alija said yes to three Bosnias on ethnic basis ..." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: So Dr. Karadzic continues as follows: "That was the first time that Alija said yes to three Bosnias on ethnic basis and that was fatal for him. The maps they showed us were completely unacceptable but Cutileiro asked us if we would accept them as the basis for future negotiations. We held on to it as the basis for future talks. It was important to us that it was divided in three, that it was on ethnic basis and that some kind of map actually exists, by which we territorialise our rights between 45 to 50 per cent. You know what Cutileiro's map looked like. That was the moment when Bosnia collapsed and we were accepted as a party to the conflict -- in the conflict. The international community made a huge mistake by sending Cutileiro and Carrington to see us before the war and by accepting us as a party in the conflict. If they had ignored us, kept silent and acknowledged Bosnia and then said afterwards that some rebels were overthrowing their own state, we would have faced difficult problems; nobody would have talked to us. By our softness" - there is a question about that precise translation - "and ability to negotiate ... it seemed to them that the Serbs would accept it at any moment. It has been like that from the beginning until now. We made them think that they would be successful if they enter the process, if they internationalise the issue of Bosnia. Because Bosnia becomes done at the moment it gets internationalised and we are recognised as a party in the conflict." Was Dr. Karadzic speaking accurately when he told the representatives in the Bosnian Serb Assembly that the critical aspect of the statement of principles on March 18th was that to the Serbs Bosnia had been divided in three and that it meant that the Bosnian Serbs had been acknowledged as a party and that therefore would not face being accused of being rebels and overthrowing their own state but that the international community would consider them a party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say so, yes. Because it was a great achievement to be a party to the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Karadzic, in the meeting on the 9th of December, 1991 that we looked at a moment ago, spoke about the need to act from -- in two ways, referring to both the legality and the factual status. And it's the case, isn't it, Mr. Krajisnik, that a few months later, when the Bosnian Serb leadership returned from the Cutileiro discussions to the Bosnian Serb Assembly on 18 March 1991, that they began to implement steps necessary to establish a de facto situation that would achieve their objectives? And when I say "they," I should say you and the other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our objective was to have a constituent unit. And you're right, from the 18th March onwards, once we reached an agreement to give up on Yugoslavia and to accept Bosnia, then for practical purposes, regionalisation in the field was accelerated, spontaneously or not spontaneously, to make sure we all knew which ethnic areas belonged to whom. Not to win these areas but to identify them so that we know what we are talking about when maps are drawn.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And in what sense is it necessary, Mr. Krajisnik, to accelerate regionalisation in a de facto manner in order to identify the territory sought by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant to identify ethnic areas, because we were given permission to make adjustments of municipalities and it was allowed to change municipalities, areas, territorially, to identify which settlement, which village was Serb, within one municipality. All sides did the same thing, Muslim, Croat and others, but I am talking only about the Serbs, in order to be able to assist the commission that was to begin that work the next day or the day after next. But maybe I should point out one more thing that could be of interest concerning the map. The map is 40 to 50 per cent, whereas your map is no more than 20. It says here that we got from Cutileiro 40 to 50 per cent of Bosnia, and in that other map that we reviewed this morning, there is no more than 25 per cent. I just want to stress it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I do not understand one part of your previous answer. You said the de facto manner in order to identify the territory. You say it was to identify which settlement, which village, was Serb within one municipality. Now, I imagine that as one way of doing it, saying at the negotiation table, "This village or that hamlet or this area, we consider to be Serb, and therefore we claim it would be part of our territory." De facto regionalisation, I understand, but please correct me if I'm wrong, that you do not say at a negotiation table this village or this hamlet is Serb but that you take a decision that it's now part of the region, whatever region that will be, but whatever Serb region, and say, this is it now. Where you create a fait accompli. That's how I understand de facto. De facto manner in order to identify by accelerating regionalisation. Tell me what is -- if I wrongly understand the distinction between de facto accelerating regionalisation by identifying, from just pointing at a certain village, hamlet, area, at the negotiation table, which asks nothing else than to say, this and this and this, without any de facto movement on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a small correction. You are right to a large extent but I want to make one small correction. Apart from the autonomous regions, we had regions on paper. They did not function, and it was well known what ethnic Serb areas were. And then we needed to identify certain small, minor ethnic territories within municipalities that were not part of those regions. So that we have arguments at the negotiating table, saying that we need to include these territories because we needed to enlarge the Serb ethnic area. That was our task, and that's what we were doing across Bosnia and Herzegovina. It just needed to be known. The negotiations had started. There was no more any working regionalisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. De facto and on paper. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe -- maybe I misused the word de facto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked whether the distinction I perceived was correct, and you said with a small correction it was. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Now, the concern that in particular that animated the interest in moving -- in implementing a de facto approach was the concern that the Muslims wanted an internationally recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina, right? And that's what you have told the members of the parliament at the March 18th, 1991 session.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of March, that agreement was reached, and it was envisaged that we could work on parts of municipalities, and we had decided what to do to implement that plan. Now, when you are discussing with people and trying to get them to accept the plan, you have to scare them a bit into accepting it, because it was a major responsibility, but our intention was to advance the preparations as much as we could and prepare the plan for implementation, because the negotiating team did not know where the Serb ethnic areas were, spread across Bosnia. How could we know that?

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And the way in which you scared them is by telling them that you thought the problem is that they, meaning the Muslims, want Bosnia and Herzegovina to be internationally recognised at all costs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we knew that, we knew that Bosnians wanted to have Bosnia internationally recognised without any transformation. But it's a different matter that we had agreed with Cutileiro to conduct the referendum after the agreement, and they agreed with us on that. You have that in the material I produced to you yesterday. But they wanted recognition without transformation. If I said that, there was nothing wrong with it, and that turned out to be true ultimately.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And that was the reason you gave the delegates for why it would be a good thing if the Bosnian Serbs could do one thing for strategic reasons, if we could start implementing what we have agreed upon, the ethnic division on the ground, and to thereafter implement a de facto ethnic division on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that more than once. We had agreed on the 18th of March, that's the agreement. I said let's implement this now. Let's identify the areas. Let's know what is ours, so that we are able to say it at negotiations. I didn't say that we Serbs should do it on the ground. My idea was to implement what had already been agreed and then see what to do next, the ethnic division as reflected in Cutileiro's principles.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, in fact, at page 13 of the English, and this was raised during the course of your examination-in-chief, you did say, "The ethnic division on the ground." And perhaps it's also useful to look at what the other deputies said after you suggested implementing the ethnic division on the ground. Let's look at page 21 of the English and page 27 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, this is, of course, the 11th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly held on March 18th, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are slightly puzzled. We don't suppose it's of any great importance, but both Mr. Josse and I heard my name mentioned. One tends to hear one's name quite naturally. But we both heard it. It doesn't appear anywhere on the transcript. It may be absolutely trivial, in which case we can ignore it, but it's best to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note Mr. Krajisnik said, "Mr. Stewart asked me about it." He speaks very fast. It's very difficult to get everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the difficulties, Your Honour. That's just -- okay. Well, that's probably, then, Your Honour, perhaps a point at which Your Honour might remind Mr. Krajisnik, once again, to serve his interests best by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just about to do that. Mr. Krajisnik, we missed although a not very important part of what you said due to the fact that the interpreters had difficulties in following your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, let me ask you to turn to page 23 through 24 of the English, page 30 through 31 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik. And the remarks of Mr. Bjelosevic. He says, in the second paragraph of his comments: "First and most importantly I would like to welcome Mrs. Plavsic's advice which she offered last time when she was speaking about Croats, which concerns the creation of a de facto situation. In this moment there is simply no reason for us to think of something new when we can use the Croatian model of political action on the ground in BH. The model consists of the following: Their armed units are occupying the areas they consider to be theirs. I suggest that we adopt the Croatian model of creating a de facto situation on the ground to continue working in the Serbian Assembly and to have the negotiating team continue its work." Mr. Perisic, on page 28 of the English, and page 37 through 38 of the B/C/S, at the very top of the page at page 28. "A very important matter," he states, "and one highlighted by many people is that a state is created in two ways, by negotiations, talks, diplomatic methods, political moves, et cetera. The other way, which is more important, entails practical moves on the ground." And I think one more reference at the moment, and that's Mr. Ijacic at page 30 of the English, and page 41 of your version in B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik. And it's at the very top of the English. "It has been stressed here that the actual situation on the ground was very important, and I would like to add that the more we achieve on the ground the less will have to be said by our negotiators to achieve more. And secondly, the more we achieve on the ground, the more time will be on our side and the negotiations can last even longer. In the opposite case, time is our enemy." Mr. Krajisnik, just as Dr. Karadzic had mentioned on December 9th, 1991, the discussion here was about attempting to achieve Bosnian Serb objectives by moving forward in two ways: Continue to negotiate but move forward to implement a de facto solution on the ground. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But not by armed force. That's not the meaning. What it means is we need to take control where we can because in many places control had not been taken of; whereas Croats had taken control using their units, and they had even crossed over into Posavina. That's what has been recorded here.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And by taking control of territories claimed to be Bosnian Serb, the Bosnian Serbs would be able to go to the negotiations and say, "This is our territory."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It's just that if you don't have control in a certain place, and the other side is physically capturing your territory, then you will end up in a situation where Europe, as it says here, might recognise the de facto situation and you will lose your territories. And it was drawn on a map. It wasn't warfare. We didn't have warfare on any -- on any territory at that time, as far as Serbs are concerned. When we create a region, that's the de facto situation, when you take control it's de facto situation. All the way until then, authorities, governments simply were not functioning, and we had the right to have our authorities in that particular municipality. I do not doubt that there are people who meant it differently, but the passage you read means what I just explained, and that's the way Karadzic thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one question, Mr. Krajisnik? You explained that the other side, if the other side is physically capturing your territory, that was a risk of this being accepted as a factual situation.
