Would that be any different for your side, physically capturing territory? Would that not create a risk for the other side then? That it would be accepted as a de facto situation? I mean, why would it be true one way and why would it not be -- exactly be true the other way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here is why, Your Honour. As it says here, forces from Croatia came in and physically captured those areas, because the warfare was going on in Croatia, in Posavina, and the deputies say, Europe might recognise the de facto situation because we had let go of power. We don't have any units on that day that we are speaking, the 18th of March, in order to go forward and take over somebody else's territories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at the same time, some of the assemblymen say, if we move on the ground, there is less need to further negotiate. I do understand that one of the basics of the negotiations were where to draw the lines. I mean, what, then, does that mean, if you say we have to negotiate less if we are making our movements on the ground or if we -- how could we understand this and also the reference to the Croatian method, as one of the assemblymen said, how could we understand that other than - please help me out - other than that if you would have created de facto situation on the ground, that it would -- might be favourable in further negotiations because the factual situation might be accepted as it was developing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is being said is that Europe could recognise the de facto situation. Croats took some territories. We did not have authority there but we were supposed to. And I'm saying, and what they are saying, and I'm explaining it, is that we did not have the -- our police or anything else there because nobody held authority there. They simply came there and they took those territories. You're right. Perhaps implicitly this MP was saying, although I didn't understand it then but I think it's correct, look at what the Croats are doing. And perhaps implicitly he was saying that some force of ours should be doing that kind of thing but we didn't have an army at the time, so we couldn't do that kind of thing. I mean I'm not trying to say that he didn't say this, but we didn't have any force at the time, and how could we issue orders to have the territories taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you understand it to be that even if they were hinting at such a thing to be done or to happen, that it could not be a real suggestion because there were no forces anyhow that could do such a thing? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what happened. We didn't have any forces that could take the territories of others then, and we did not take any territories. So yes, you're right. They were worried because Croats were taking territories, as they put it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you just said "we didn't have any force at the time," and asked rhetorically how could we issue orders to have the territories taken? At page 36 of the English and page 53 of your version in B/C/S, Mr. Vjestica begins to speak, and says, at page 38 of the English, in about the fourth paragraph, that's still page 53 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik: "We need to establish the authorities and the Serbian state of BH." He mentioned a couple of particular things that need to be done, "arrangements for the next session and for implementing the constitution we have adopted. Implementing all the laws we have adopted." And then he states: "In addition to these two conditions, we must urgently establish a Serbian MUP in the Republic of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina. We must establish national defence. Our Serbian army, which is already there on the ground, we just need to transform it into what we need to have." At the bottom of the page on 38, he offers Bosanska Krupa as a textbook example, noting in the very last sentence of the English: "We have de facto occupied our own territories." And then states: "Mr. President, I think that you have to give us an order that after the next assembly, you should order this, that we arrange it for the areas where it has not been done and to implement this, that the Serbs should occupy their territories so that no other forces could enter them. Thank you." In urging the establishment, indeed the need to urgently establish a Serbian MUP in the Republic of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Vjestica was making reference to his concern about what you just said, that at that moment, your quote was, "We didn't have any force at the time, and how could we issue orders to have the territories taken?" Is that right? That's the gist of Mr. Vjestica's concern at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, a correction. It's not Mr. Chairman, what it says here, it's Mr. President, and he probably meant Karadzic because he was the president and he was present. Also in response to your question, all of this was explained by Mr. Vjestica in your interview. I can just repeat what he thought, that -- or, rather, he denied all of this. Obviously --

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I know.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: I understand precisely what you're telling us. You said in response to an earlier question by the Court, that at that time we didn't have any force and how could we issue orders to have the territories taken? You were present at March 18th, 1991, at the 11th Session, when Vjestica said this. And by --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. And we didn't have any forces that we could issue such orders to. And this is not correct. I did not know about this. What he was saying was just -- well, how should I put this -- an exaggeration of his own territory. We didn't have any forces. The JNA was there.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Vjestica is urging the establishment of such forces including, and in particular, the MUP, for just that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- I mean yes. But we adopted a law, and he is saying let's form a MUP as soon as possible, and we didn't form one until the end of March, until the war started. There were different proposals. I agree with you there were different proposals. But we did not have an armed force of our own that we could issue orders to. At least I did not know about any such thing. How can I know whether somebody had something on a local level?

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: You mentioned the comment about Mr. -- or that Mr. Vjestica directed his remarks at the end of his comments to Mr. President. Mr. Krajisnik, this probably won't come as news to you in view of the many, many sessions over which you presided, but it appears, looking at this session in particular, that you call on -- you give an order of -- by which people will be called upon and speak. Everyone rises and says, "Mr. President, Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen," that's all directed to you, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You see what this was all about. Although this was not correct, I know who Mr. Vjestica considered to be the Supreme Commander at the time, although there was no war on. But you're quite right, I was chairing that session and everybody was addressing me as Mr. President, as of Mr. President of the Assembly. However, I'm sure that he meant Karadzic, as far as issuing orders was concerned. But even if he addressed me, it doesn't matter. I was not in charge of that. I could not do that. But he considered Karadzic to be the top person, although he was only president of the party. I'm saying that for the sake of the truth. It's not that I'm trying to disassociate myself.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Now, as you said here at page 59, line 7: "We didn't form a MUP until the end of March, until the war started." And you were asked during the course of your examination-in-chief about the establishment of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tell you what I meant, if you want. When this dispatch was sent by Mr. Mandic. That's what I meant. That's what I meant. That's what I was referring to. That was the end of March, beginning of April. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: So Mr. Mandic's dispatch, then, represented the formation of the Bosnian Serb MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. I'm saying that up until that moment, there was a joint MUP, and I indicated something that was debatable here, that was in dispute, because the MUP split up. And then at just one moment -- I was saying that before that there shouldn't have been a separate Serbian MUP, although a minister had been appointed on the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, a separate, Serbian, Bosnian Serb MUP came into effect on April 1st or March 31st, depending on how you count, that is eight days from the promulgation of the law on internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I was quite precise. At Vjestica's proposal to establish a MUP, I said that we had not established a MUP until the end of March, and I meant a particular point in time. Mr. Mandic's dispatch. Up until that moment, it certainly had not been formed. And when it was actually formed, you can see that in documents, certainly. You can find all of that when it was established and so on and so forth. But I am saying that up until the end of March, nothing was done. Until the war broke out there wasn't a MUP, for sure. Or that's what it looks like here, too.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Well, perhaps there is some confusion, so let's get it clarified. I understood you during the course of your examination-in-chief to be essentially suggesting that Mr. Mandic's dispatch represented some kind of irresponsible or unauthorised action by a single individual or maybe two individuals contrary to the wishes of you and Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct. That's exactly what I said. And I'm saying now that that is true as well. He did this in an unauthorised way. And it didn't really result in any effects because Mr. Delimustafic had him replaced.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: The fact, Mr. Krajisnik, is that Mr. Mandic's dispatch did nothing more than essentially recite the terms of the law on internal affairs; that is, simply recite what the Bosnian Serb Assembly enacted and what you signed, which came into effect on April 1st, 1992, thereby splitting up the joint MUP.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained that that was not true. That Mr. Mandic made some mistakes. He said that Bijeljina was the centre rather than Ugljevik. And he didn't have the right to do that. It's the government that has to do that. The government should have done that. I'm not trying to say that the law was not passed, but it was the government that was supposed to do that. We discussed that last time. Why he was not authorised to do that. Even the minister could not do that without the government. To this day, I think that was irresponsible. He shouldn't have done this. He had some reason. Well ...

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Mr. Krajisnik, we didn't discuss it. I think you and Mr. Stewart discussed it, and it's a matter I'd like to now raise with you in somewhat more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be moving on to that topic. I don't know if you would like me to begin or if you would like to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it might take some time. Although I hope that -- not too much. Therefore, we'll first have a break now until quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If the next bundle has not been distributed yet, I'd ask that that be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, before the adjournment, or the break, I had suggested to you that the dispatch sent by Momcilo Mandic on 31 March 1992 represented essentially a recitation of the state of affairs, that is the law that had been enacted by the Assembly and signed by you with respect to the establishment of a Bosnian Serb MUP. And perhaps the best way of addressing that is simply to look at the dispatch, which is found at tab 92. And although normally a comprehensive review of or line by line review of a document is not feasible logistically, in this case we have a relatively short document so I think we can try to do that. So let me ask you first to begin at the beginning. Mr. Mandic's dispatch says: "At its meeting held on 27 March 1992, the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in accordance with the political orientation of the Serbian people and the Sarajevo agreement, promulgated the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." That's correct, right? That's simply a recitation of what happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes. The constitution of the Serb republic was promulgated.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: "In addition, the Assembly of the Serbian People passed a number of laws and other regulations necessary for the functioning of the Republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In that respect, it passed a Law on Internal Affairs, which shall be uniformly applied on the territory of the Republic of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina as of 1 April 1992, and appointed Mico Stanisic, until now an adviser in the Bosnian MUP, as minister." And it is correct, is it not, Mr. Krajisnik, that on the 28th of February, 1992 the Bosnian Serb Assembly passed the Law on Internal Affairs, and at its 13th Session on March 24th, 1992 the -- Mr. Stanisic was appointed as Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: "This Law, among other things," the dispatch continues, "regulates a unified Public Security Service, regulates and organises the National Security Service within the framework of the rights and duties of the Republic of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, regulates the duties and powers of MUP employees, mutual relationships and cooperation between the organs of the Interior, and the education, professional training and specialist training of employees." And that's simply an accurate account of the Law on Internal Affairs, perhaps not fully comprehensive but accurate in capturing its gist?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And the dispatch continues: "In order to conduct internal affairs on the territory of the Republic of Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Minister of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, based in Sarajevo, is setting up the following Security Services Centres as territorial units: Banja Luka, for the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina;. Trebinje, for the area of the Serbian Autonomous District of Herzegovina;. Doboj, for the area of Serbian Autonomous District of Northern Bosnia;. Sarajevo for the area of Romanija-Birac Serbian Autonomous District;. Ugljevik, for the area of the Serbian Autonomous District of Semberija." And as you've noted before, and have stressed more than once, Ugljevik was, as you said it, I think -- you said Bijeljina was in play rather than Ugljevik. And if we look to Article 28 of the Law on Internal Affairs, we see that Mr. Mandic's dispatch faithfully recites the first four, although Northern Bosnia is not there. But you are correct that the Law on Internal Affairs -- which is found at tab 91, Your Honours. Article 28 states: Bijeljina for the territory of the Serbian Autonomous District Semberija rather than Ugljevik. Now, Mr. Mandic -- Mr. Mandic, excuse me, Mr. Krajisnik. Can you turn, please, to tab 94 and take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know. I mean, I think he corrected that later.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Tab 94, which does need a number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1202.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Is a letter sent or dated 16 April 1992 from Mr. Mandic, the Deputy Minister of the Bosnian Serb MUP, to Predrag Jesuric at the Public Security Station, Bijeljina. And in it Mr. Mandic states: "At a meeting of the Professional Collegium of the Serbian MUP held on 16 April 1992, it was proposed that the Majevica and Semberija security -- CSB, or Security Services Centre be established in Bijeljina rather than in Ugljevik, since Bijeljina has better material and technical equipment and a more substantial human potential. "A proposal was sent to the government to correct what was most probably a misprint in the Law on the Interior of the Serbian Republic of the BH. "Carry out all preparations in connection with the takeover of the CSB and inform the government of Majevica and Semberija." So it would seem, Mr. Krajisnik, that the simple answer to the discrepancy between Ugljevik and Bijeljina in Mr. Mandic's dispatch rests in what is reflected in the letter of April 16th, that he had either a different version of the law or an earlier draft or something that led him to believe that the Law on the Interior inaccurately, as he noted there, indicated Ugljevik rather than Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the seat of Semberija, Majevica, that SAO, was in Ugljevik, and he referred to that just by way of an automatic response. That's the reason why he mentioned Ugljevik. It wasn't Bijeljina at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: No, that's not what the letter of April 16th seems to indicate. It indicates instead that Mr. Mandic believes that there was a misprint in the Law on the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you, in the law it says Bijeljina. However, when he wrote that paper, he probably looked at the seats of different regions, and he said Ugljevik. In the decision on the establishment of Semberija and Majevica, it says that Ugljevik is the seat of that region. That's what I assume. I don't know what other reason he could have had. It's not a misprint. He simply made a mistake. He didn't look at the law. He simply looked at the seats of autonomous regions.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Well, the Court will be able to determine what prompted Mr. Mandic to indicate Ugljevik rather than Bijeljina. But at a minimum, Mr. Krajisnik, it does seem to be the case, doesn't it, that Mr. Mandic, who has been faithfully reciting the law up to the point he lists the Security Services Centres that will be set up as territorial units, was attempting to do precisely the same in listing the locations of those Security Services Centre. He was simply trying to follow the law. And when he found out there was a discrepancy he wrote the government and said there was a misprint. Now, whether correct or not, that's pretty clearly what he was trying to do there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But he couldn't have sent the dispatch before that, before he got an answer from the government. I hope. And now he's sending this to the government? And before that, as deputy minister, he had already issued instructions in order to have this corrected. He should have presented this to the government, if that's important. As deputy minister, he could not have done any of the two. On the 16th of April he's deputy minister. And before April he was completely unauthorised.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: The point, Mr. Krajisnik, as I indicated more than once when we were going over this, is that Mr. Mandic's dispatch is not an attempt by him to engage in any unauthorised unilateral action but merely a recitation of the law, as he understands it, which will come into effect on the dates he indicates. But let's continue with the rest of the dispatch. "Within the above-mentioned Security Services Centres, in order to carry out specific tasks and duties within the competence of the organs of internal affairs, Public Security Stations are set up for the territories of municipalities." And that's correct, too; nothing controversial about that, right? You're looking at me, Mr. Krajisnik, but that's -- I'm reading from the first sentence of the third paragraph of the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem is that he couldn't have sent this. That's the only thing that's a problem. And this law could not enter into force before the constitution entered into force.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: We'll look at the -- when the law enters into force in just a moment, but let's take it one step at a time. So. I take it that your answer indirectly is an affirmation of the question I posed to you that there is -- that that sentence that I read to you is also legally accurate and just a recitation of what the Law on Internal Affairs provides?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is no controversy there. Everything that he says in the dispatch is more or less in accordance with the law. Perhaps there is something that's exceptional but that is of no importance. Even Ugljevik is of no importance.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Now, next sentence says: "On the day this Law comes into force, the Security Services Centres and Public Security Stations of the Serbian Republic of" -- I'm sorry -- "of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina MUP," that is the joint MUP, and then continuing, "on the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina are abolished and cease to function, and their authority, that is, tasks and duties within the competence of organs of internal affairs are taken over by the above-mentioned organisational units of MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And that, Mr. Krajisnik, is simply a recitation of Article 126, the Law on Internal Affairs, isn't it? And please turn your attention to tab 91, Article 126.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's found at page 30 of the English, Your Honours, and page 01138938 in the B/C/S. And it states: "On the day of entry into force of this" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is it really necessary to read it again? I mean, we can read it more quickly than the translators can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Great, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik can read it as well.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: So that second sentence of Mr. Mandic's third paragraph in the dispatch is simply a recitation of Article 126?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but I mean -- well, yes, I confirm that all of that is from the law. There is no need for you to move on this way gradually. There is no dispute about that, that he had the law before him, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: So the entire dispatch, with the exception of that minor discrepancy involving Ugljevik and Bijeljina is a simple and faithful recitation of the law enacted by the Bosnian Serb Assembly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that has been confirmed by now. Let's try to move on a bit more -- I do understand, Mr. Tieger, that you wanted to take it step by step but if you could make the step a bit more -- a bit shorter.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And that law, Mr. Krajisnik, was self-implementing. It came in effect eight days from the promulgation -- from its promulgation on March 23rd, 1992, and there was no dispute that it was promulgated on that date, as you indicated in your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I did not say that. I said it is written there, eight days after promulgation. But I didn't know when it would be promulgated or when somebody would place it in the Official Gazette. And I said that within 15 days, organisation would be done, and Mr. Mandic did all that in his dispatch.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: To whom did you say -- okay. So the reference about organisation being done within 15 days, that's another reference to the fact that since regulations had not been promulgated that rendered the -- what would otherwise appear to be the self-implementing provisions of the Law on Internal Affairs null and void, or at least not in force?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This law should have been given by the minister to the government, the government should have endorsed the method of organisation, after which this dispatch would be sent, and centres were envisaged by the law. He shouldn't have done all this by himself, even if he had been minister. He should have consulted the government. I think I have said this previously in my examination.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the constitution of the Serbian Republic entered into effect on the day it was promulgated, didn't it? That's provided in the constitution, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, every lawyer knows this has to be published in the Official Gazette and that somebody has to enforce it. We never approved, we never endorsed, those minutes of that Assembly session. On the 27th of March, we didn't endorse any minutes of the Assembly session. Only then could it have been promulgated.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, you were president of the Bosnian Serb Assembly responsible for the enacting -- for overseeing the preparation and enactment and implementation of the legislation emerging from that body. We are now looking at a piece of legislation that states explicitly in its provisions when and how it comes into effect. Now, you've told us that among the reasons why those provisions should not be relied upon is Article 129, which refers to the regulations of the Law on Internal Affairs. First of all, Article 129: "General acts on the internal organisation of the Ministry and the National Security Service shall be adopted not later than within 15 days of the entry of this law into force," is what I guess we lawyers would call a condition subsequent, and something I suspect was familiar to you as a legislator. That is, it can't prevent the law from coming into effect; it's only meaningful after the law comes into effect. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, with all due respect, that's not the way it is. It's stated in the constitution that we worked on the 27th, that we may do the linking up in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We took that to Brussels. It wasn't published. It wasn't promulgated. All those were moves that would leave us some room. If that law were to be enacted, it would apply to the Serbian MUP within our constituent unit, not in isolation. Find it in the constitution and you will see that that's the way it's stipulated and that was supposed to be endorsed as part of the minutes and the problem would have been solved. All this is linked to the issue of promulgation, which is something I know nothing about. That was a job done by technical services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber thinks that this repeated course in constitutional law and the technique of implementing laws has been sufficient for the time being, and the Chamber is also aware that it should look both at the formal legal aspects of these matters, which have been very much emphasised by Mr. Krajisnik, and also on what actually happened, even if it would not fulfil all the legal requirements. But to spend more time on this aspect doesn't seem to assist the Chamber at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I hope the next couple of exhibits I turn the Court to won't run afoul of that guidance. I apologise in advance if it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you can do it, if you say this is a document saying so and so, Mr. Krajisnik, would this support or would this not support, then we know what we are talking about, but if every document and every question takes us ten minutes, then the Chamber might write a thesis on constitutional law soon.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, please turn to page 93 -- to tab 93. That's the decision on proclaiming the constitutional law for implementation of the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in particular please turn to Article 12, which states: "Until the" -- well, you can read it, but it is basically an article stating that until regulations are passed, the laws and regulations of the Serbian -- the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be applied. That's a reflection, Mr. Krajisnik, isn't it, of the fact that in getting this -- these organs and authorities off the ground, there wasn't time to write all the regulations necessary for their functioning and it was in fact perhaps pointless not to adopt many, if not most, of those that had been used over the years in such institutions as the joint MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That's not the way it is. On the contrary, it says quite the opposite here. It is meant that once the constitutional law and the constitution are proclaimed, pending the adoption of new laws, the legislation of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be applied, as long as they are not contrary to the laws of Republika Srpska. It's the same date but the proclamation of both enactments was on the 27th of March. Both of them were adopted on the 28th of February. I mean they were passed on the 28th of February, but somebody published them ...

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And in fact, Mr. Krajisnik, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see. Mr. Krajisnik referred to the 27th of March. It looks as although it is not part of the translation, that it was published the 16th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said the 28th of February. Yes, the 16th of March it was published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not the 27th but the 16th. Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And in fact, Mr. Krajisnik, we've heard previous evidence in this case that the regulations for the internal organisation of the Bosnian Serb MUP were not adopted until at the earliest September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, which regulations? Yugoslav and Bosnian regulations were applied in the meantime. That's not a problem. I don't know what regulations you are referring to, but I would be happy to answer. Because we said that we would adopt all positive legislation, both of Yugoslavia and of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: I believe you've answered the question, Mr. Krajisnik, and that is that until the adoption of regulations for the Bosnian Serb MUP in September of 1992, that the previous regulations applied. Now, in fact, Mr. Krajisnik, the -- in the field, people were waiting not for any dispatch by Mr. Mandic or any unilateral action by any minister or deputy minister of the Bosnian Serb government, but were waiting to be notified that the Law on Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had in fact come into effect. And in that connection, sir, please turn to tab 95. Tab 95, P763.C tab 67, is a report dated March 23rd, 1992 from the State Security Service of the Federal Secretariat of Internal Affairs, reporting about findings and observations in a number of areas. If you could turn to page 8 of the English and page 8 of your version, both at the top. That report indicates --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, because I am completely confident that you will catch this, it appears that the first most of the first three sentences in English are some kind of transposition from another document. They don't appear to have any relationship to that. We'll have to get that addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Starting with the words "were attempts."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's one. And then up until?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "The situation." It doesn't appear to be any kind of comprehensible segue from the previous point. In any event, as you can see the -- part 3 on the previous page begins "Bosanska Krupa" and although I haven't had it specifically translated, it would seem to start at "situation in the area of Bosanska Krupa municipality."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And the report states: "Reserve police of the Serb municipality Bosanska Krupa (about 200 men) and the rest of active and reserve police of Serb nationality from this area have occupied the roads and the posts on the right bank of Una River in order to forestall any possible events. Lately they have been ready to block the critical territories within the town itself for the purpose of division should the decision on merging with Banja Luka region and CSB Banja Luka become effective. Other than that, during our last contact in Banja Luka on March 3rd this year, chief of CSB Banja Luka informed us that such decision was not going to be implemented before the Law on Internal Affairs of the Serb Republic Bosnia comes into effect." Now, first of all, Mr. Krajisnik, the reference to the chief of CSB Banja Luka, that's a reference to Stojan Zupljanin; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. At that time he was both in the Bosnian and in our MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And do you have any reason to dispute that what Mr. Zupljanin was waiting for, in order to implement the decision to block the critical territories for the purpose of division, was for the Law on Internal Affairs to come into effect?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand that this is a reference to Mr. Zupljanin having done that, but the Bosnian -- but the police from Bosanska Krupa, that they took control of it on their own initiative. I mean the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Well, maybe you need me to ask to you look at the document a little more carefully and then we'll leave it but it clearly says --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the following passage where Mr. Zupljanin said on the 5th of March that -- otherwise this would not be applied pending the adoption of the Law on Internal Affairs, meaning the annexation of the Security Services Centre or Public Security Station, that they would not annex it until the law is enacted. This concerns, I don't know, maybe the division of the MUP -- no, sorry, MUP and the outside territory. This is a brief from the 13th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, the question has been answered. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Now, one of the other things that you said when addressing this issue during the course of your examination-in-chief was that, as dismayed as you and Dr. Karadzic were by Mr. Mandic's dispatch, there wasn't really time to do anything about it, to clarify that it had not been the intention of Bosnian Serb leaders to split the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I said they couldn't do anything because war started very soon afterwards. There was no time to do anything after the 31st because the war started almost immediately afterwards. That was the point of what I said. I didn't say that we were not going to divide MUP. We wanted our own MUP within Bosnia and Herzegovina, in line with the Cutileiro principles because that's what we had a right to. But we didn't want to do it arbitrarily. We wanted to do it according to the principles.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Well, if you'll turn to tab 96, we'll see that there was certainly time for Mr. Stanisic to verify and underscore Mr. Mandic's dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1203.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Now, this was sent by Mico Stanisic on the 3rd of April, 1992 to all CSBs and to all SJBs, and it concerns information that Mr. Stanisic has received to the effect that a dispatch with Momo Mandic's signature has been sent out on behalf of the Serb Republic of BiH MUP inviting all Department of Internal Affairs employees to return to their regular jobs and posts. And in the second paragraph, Mr. Stanisic states that: "... this is an already established way of misinforming and waging a special war on behalf of individual management employees of the ex-MUP," and informing the employees of the Serb Republic of BiH Ministry of Interior not to fall for such tricks and misinformation. And concluding: "We are warning again to abide by the Serb Republic of BiH constitution and Law on Internal Affairs as well as the orders issued by Mico Stanisic, Minister of Interior."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a reference to some sort of dispatch of the 3rd April, that is a forgery, signed by Mr. Mandic, urging everybody to go back to their jobs. So Stanisic, referring to that dispatch, tells people not to fall for that provocation. It's not the same dispatch sent by Mr. Mandic that we discussed a moment ago. But he, Stanisic, was probably aware of that other dispatch that was sent in end March that was in dispute. At least at this moment he knew about it.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: He clearly knew about it, and in fact, what he's referring to as you indicate is -- and what you indicate was a forgery, was that someone sent something out very quickly apparently after Mr. Mandic's dispatch, attempting to effectively rescind it. You were asked by the Chamber why, if you and Dr. Karadzic so adamantly were against this unauthorised and irresponsible action by Mr. Mandic, you didn't send out a dispatch or notice that it was, in fact, unauthorised and irresponsible, and your answer was that there wasn't sufficient time and the war events overtook the opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there are several questions in that one. I just wish to explain, here in paragraph 1, it says that somebody sent a false dispatch under the name of Mr. Mandic. Well, several questions were asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's focus on the most important one. The issue Mr. Tieger raises is the following. You said we had no time, the war was about to start, started, we had no time to respond to what you called an irresponsible dispatch of Mr. Mandic. The question now is that if a couple of days later, another false dispatch is sent, how it could be that you found time to respond to that and not to the earlier one, although the war was even closer. That's, I take it, Mr. Tieger, the issue you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please answer to that and focus on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's all intertwined. Everything is mixed up, Your Honour. Please, I know exactly what I said and I can explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd rather first have an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Delimustafic who reacted to Mr. Mandic's dispatch. He cancelled it and he replaced Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So now your answer is that because some other action had been taken, there was no need to respond to it anymore. Is that -- is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It's just that when Delimustafic sent out his notice we just had only one day to agree with the Muslims how to deal with the problem. This was on the 3rd. I'm just saying that we had only two days from Delimustafic's reaction until the war. We had only two days to sit down and deal with the problem, whereas on a parallel track the conference was going on. We were working on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now Mr. Tieger's question was even if you had so little time, why was there time to respond to the forged dispatch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what the minister did, whereas we sat down with the Muslim side in Lisbon and we discussed this dispatch and we said we would continue negotiations, and Delimustafic rendered it null and void. However, negotiations did not continue. Instead the war started. And Republika Srpska took this path.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be finishing with this subject soon. I think Mr. Harmon needs a couple of minutes, or Mr. Josse, one of the two, and although I probably need only about ten or 15 more minutes on this subject, I don't think it's a good idea to begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've only five and a half minutes left. Mr. Harmon, Mr. Josse, who is to take the initiative?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will take the initiative. Yesterday, in court, in respect of Exhibit 1193, Prosecution exhibit, the Defence posed a question why we didn't put that exhibit in our case in chief, why we didn't rely on it. We had that document before and during the course of our case in chief. We disclosed it twice to the Defence. There was a question raised by the Defence that an inference could be drawn that we purposely withheld that document so we could ambush the defendant with it should he take the stand. I simply state that categorically that was not the case. Unfortunately, with the tens of thousands of documents that we review, we came to the realisation that the contents of this document only when we were preparing for the cross-examination of Mr. Krajisnik. We have produced considerable evidence in respect of Variant A and Variant B in the course of our case in chief. We are not going to rely on this particular document, and we are prepared to withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I, of course, accept the assurance that my learned friend has just given to the Chamber and, in effect, the Defence, that no ambush was intended, and, of course, I welcome the withdrawal of that particular exhibit from the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, you are instructed to vacate the number P1193 and to return the exhibit to the Prosecution. And we'll destroy our copies of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have one small matter. Your Honour, I wonder if we might have the Court's permission on Tuesday, when we resume and sit in the afternoon, to see Mr. Krajisnik before court. It wouldn't affect the starting time. It's much easier to see him before than after actually. Could we see him say at half past 1.00 just for, well, those ten minutes or so? Of course, Your Honour, not to impinge upon his evidence at all but a number of practical matters as to the future planning of the case beyond his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it's just about practical matters, Mr. Tieger, I take it that there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When I say "practical matters," Your Honour, of course I don't want to mislead. It may touch on aspects of the case itself but not his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I mean, Mr. Stewart is aware of the boundaries of appropriate discussion, and I have no doubt he'll follow those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart, that's no problem. Mr. Tieger, you said, of course, you know that Mr. Stewart is aware of the restrictions that are there at this moment. I'd like to add to that - and I'm addressing you, Mr. Krajisnik - that you should also be fully aware of the restrictions that are applicable at this moment, which would include any telephone conversation with any person, member of a team on investigative matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I just want to clarify something. When my mother asks me how are you doing, I say fine. But, if I'm not supposed to talk to the members of my team, just tell me, and I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not about anything that is related to this case, and if there is contact to members of the team, which we clearly set the conditions. The conditions were that counsel and members of the team would not have any contact with any -- with an investigator at a certain moment. That, of course, would be true for you as well, in the capacity of that person, as a member of the team, and I take it that asking to find documents is a matter which directly relates to the case and is beyond a private atmosphere. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I need to make something clear, Your Honour. And Mr. Krajisnik probably won't know this, but I gave instruction to Mr. Sladojevic yesterday to contact yesterday one of the investigators but not the investigator whom Your Honour had forbidden us to speak to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about Mr. Krajisnik himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was a little concerned about what Your Honour had just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just talking about Mr. Krajisnik himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. And I set up the parameters extremely clearly to Mr. Sladojevic and he relayed that to the investigator concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Mr. Sladojevic. I'm not talking about Defence counsel. I'm just talking about telephone conversations from Mr. Krajisnik himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my understanding was that I could not discuss the case, that I cannot discuss my testimony or anything I will say in my testimony in the future. And if I cannot talk at all, just tell me. I won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I was just saying that requests or instructions to discover documents or potential exhibits falls within the scope of what is at this moment what should not be discussed with members of the team, unless --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless consent has been given by the Chamber. I just want to explain that to you clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... full understanding of what the limits were, were assumed, and the Chamber received information that it might not have been fully understood. So that has now been addressed. We adjourn until next Tuesday. Of course, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I just inquire, just a reference to the Chamber receiving information that might not have been fully understood. I'm not aware of any information having been conveyed in court. May we receive clarification as to what that is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then, perhaps go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour. I can see that might be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We adjourn until next Tuesday, quarter past 2.00. And, of course, Mr. Josse, if it can be arranged for to see Mr. Krajisnik before that session, the Chamber has no objection whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I wish everyone a good weekend, a little bit longer than usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
